description: We are a team of five Computer Systems Engineering students from Palestine Polytechnic University, passionate about AI, software development, and innovation.Our project, Field Shift, uses NASA Earth observation data to help farmers make smarter crop rotation decisions and support sustainable agriculture. Our team combines skills in programming, AI, data analysis, research,and UI/UX design. We aim to develop a practical,innovative, and user-friendly solution to real-world agricultural challenges.
summary:
Our project, AstroRoot, is a smart agricultural decision-support platform designed to help farmers make better decisions about crop rotation and water management. We developed a tool that combines NASA Earth observation data with soil information to analyze environmental conditions and explore suitable crop rotation strategies. The platform uses historical climate data from NASA POWER and soil data from USDA SSURGO to evaluate the relationship between weather conditions, soil characteristics, and crop requirements.

AstroRoot focuses on comparing crops such as corn, soybean, and sorghum, helping farmers understand their water needs and how different rotation choices may affect their fields. By presenting this information through interactive maps, comparisons, and reports, our platform makes complex environmental data easier to understand and use.

We believe this project is important because climate change, water scarcity, and changing weather patterns create serious challenges for agriculture. Our goal is to support more informed farming decisions, encourage sustainable practices, conserve water, and help farmers build more resilient agricultural systems.
details:
Our project, AstroRoot, is a web-based agricultural decision-support platform that helps farmers understand their land and choose suitable crops based on available water resources, soil conditions, and historical climate data. We developed this platform to make agricultural decisions easier and more reliable by bringing together information from different scientific sources in one place.

How does it work?

The user starts by adding a farm location through an interactive map, GPS, or coordinates. The system then collects environmental and soil information related to that location. We use NASA POWER to obtain historical daily weather data, including temperature, rainfall, humidity, wind speed, and solar radiation. We also use USDA SSURGO soil data to understand soil layers, water-holding capacity, and other important soil characteristics.

After collecting the data, our system analyzes approximately 25 years of historical weather conditions. It then uses scientific calculations based on the FAO-56 methodology to estimate crop water requirements and irrigation needs. We compare three crops: corn, soybean, and sorghum. The system evaluates how each crop performs under different historical seasons, considering both rain-fed and irrigated conditions. Finally, it presents the results in a simple comparison that helps farmers understand which crop requires less irrigation and how often water shortages occurred in previous seasons.

Main features and benefits

We included several features to make AstroRoot useful and easy to understand. Farmers can create farm profiles, explore interactive maps, compare crop rotation plans, and view soil information through a visual soil-layer representation. We also added historical season comparisons so users can understand how different crops performed under past weather conditions.

Another feature is Ask AstroRoot, which allows users to ask questions about their results and receive explanations based on the available information. We also included an option to contact an agricultural expert, save private field notes, and generate downloadable reports containing the analysis, data sources, and scientific methods.

These features help farmers understand complex environmental information without having to deal directly with scientific datasets or complicated equations. They can compare alternatives before making decisions and better understand the possible irrigation requirements of their fields.

Tools and technologies

We developed AstroRoot using several web technologies and programming tools. For the frontend, we used HTML, CSS, and JavaScript to build the user interface and interactive features. For the backend, we used Python with FastAPI to process requests, collect external data, and perform the scientific calculations.

We used SQLite to store information such as user accounts, farm profiles, field notes, and analysis results. For interactive maps, we used MapLibre GL JS, together with NASA GIBS map layers to display rainfall and soil-moisture information. We also integrated external APIs, including NASA POWER and USDA Soil Data Access, to retrieve the environmental and soil data needed by the system.

In addition, we used Docker to support application deployment and tools such as Vercel and Render for hosting the platform. We also integrated an optional AI-powered chat feature to help explain analysis results using available evidence.

Creativity and innovation

What makes AstroRoot different is that we do not simply display weather information or satellite images. We connect NASA observations with local soil characteristics, crop water requirements, and the farmer's own priorities to produce meaningful crop comparisons.

One of the creative parts of our project is replaying 25 historical growing seasons for different crops on the same field. This allows farmers to compare alternatives using consistent environmental conditions instead of depending on only one season. We also designed a visual soil profile that helps users understand the relationship between rainfall, soil water capacity, root depth, and crop water consumption.

We wanted to make scientific information understandable and useful for people who may not have an agricultural or technical background. Our goal was to turn complex scientific calculations into clear information that can support real decisions.

Factors considered and intended impact

During development, our team considered several important factors, including water availability, rainfall patterns, temperature, soil properties, crop characteristics, irrigation requirements, and long-term climate variability. We also considered the importance of data quality, accurate calculations, transparency, and making the platform accessible on mobile devices.

Our main goal is to help farmers use water more efficiently, make better crop rotation decisions, protect soil resources, and become more prepared for changing climate conditions. We also hope the platform can help agricultural researchers and experts explore environmental information and compare different farming strategies.

AstroRoot is currently a research prototype focused on the 50 U.S. states, and its results are historical comparisons rather than guaranteed predictions or irrigation instructions. We believe that combining NASA Earth observations with agricultural science can create valuable opportunities for sustainable farming. Through this project, we wanted to show how data collected from space can be transformed into practical solutions that help people on Earth.
